# Effect size summary

d = -0.29, 95% confidence interval[-0.40,-0.18] based on N = 1,380

# Summary of the analysis approach 

The SMARVUS dataset$^1$ was initially cleaned by removing columns that were not relevant to the research question. Demographic and educational information, such as gender, language and previous level of mathematics study, was retained alongside questionnaire responses for further exploration.

The respondents were then filtered. Only students whose grades were provided directly by their universities were included to ensure consistency in comparisons, as self-reported grades could describe modules sat years before the questionnaire. Observations where grades were recorded as zero were also  excluded, as these could be null submissions.

The 70 respondents who did not fully complete all four mathematics and statistics anxiety questionnaires were also excluded to ensure consistency when calculating and comparing anxiety scores. England and Northern Ireland were grouped together to simplify geographical comparison. Furthermore, respondents who failed any of the attention checks, or who did not confirm that they had answered the survey truthfully, were excluded. This resulted in the exclusion of another 342 respondents. 8 further respondents from York University were removed due to two grades being reported by the university. 

This left a final sample of 1,380 respondents across 18 universities in 10 countries, with questionnaires completed in seven languages. Two universities had two separate IDs, which were combined into one. The geographical distribution of the final sample is presented in Table 1.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="40%"}
knitr::include_graphics("country_table.png")
```
\caption{Distribution of filtered respondents by country and survey language.}
\end{table}

The relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment was investigated using a meta-analysis, treating each university as a separate study. This approach was chosen to account for differences in grading systems and allow for investigation of variation in effect sizes across universities.

# Details of the analysis

## Accounting for differences in grading systems

A key challenge when comparing attainment in statistics modules across universities is the diversity of grading systems. Some universities use percentage-based grades, whilst others use alternative numerical scales or letter-based grading systems. Furthermore, the same percentage attainment may correspond to different levels of achievement across universities.

By treating each university as a separate study, the original numerical grading scales can be retained, avoiding the potential loss of information associated with converting all grades to a common scale.

The letter-based grading systems were treated as ordered factors, as were the grades on scales of 1-5. The percentage-based grades and grades on scales of 1-20 were treated as numerical variables. Due to Spearman's correlation measuring monotonic relationships rather than purely linear and using ranked values, it was deemed as preferable to using Pearson's correlation$^2$.

## Calculating anxiety scores

The SMARVUS dataset contains four measures of statistics and mathematics anxiety (STARS, R-MARS-S, STARS-M, & R-MARS). STARS and R-MARS-S measure statistics anxiety, whilst STARS-M and R-MARS measure mathematics anxiety. Each questionnaire consists of either 20 or 23 items, with responses recorded on a five-point scale. The overall anxiety scores were calculated by summing the individual responses for each questionnaire, with higher scores indicating greater levels of anxiety. STARS was selected as the primary measure of statistics anxiety for this analysis, as it directly measures anxiety in statistics-related situations.


## Preliminary analysis: University of Sussex

The University of Sussex was initially selected as a case study to demonstrate the approach before extending it to the wider dataset. Following the data cleaning and filtering process outlined above, 320 responses from the University of Sussex were retained. Grades at this university were reported as percentages, allowing for a direct investigation of the relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment. 

Descriptive statistics were calculated for both STARS scores and academic attainment. The mean STARS score was 70.09, with a standard deviation of 18.20 and a median of 70. Histograms were produced to further investigate the shape, spread and symmetry of both distributions.


```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 7, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment at the University of Sussex."}
sussex_histograms()
```

Figure 1 shows the distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment at the University of Sussex. The distribution of STARS scores is approximately symmetrical and bell-shaped, centred around a mean of 70.09. In contrast, the distribution of academic attainment is negatively skewed, with most respondents achieving grades between 60% and 80%. A small number of considerably lower grades contribute to the longer left tail. These observations are worth considering when investigating the correlation between statistics anxiety and academic attainment, as extreme values may influence Pearson's correlation coefficient.

Having explored the distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment individually, a scatterplot was produced to investigate the relationship between the two variables. It was hypothesised that higher levels of statistics anxiety would be associated with lower academic attainment.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, fig.cap="Scatterplot of attainment vs statistical anxiety at the University of Sussex."}
sussex_scatterplot
```

Figure 2 shows a slight negative correlation between STARS Score and attainment, suggesting that respondents with higher levels of statistical anxiety tend to perform worse. Spearman's correlation coefficient, a measure of the strength and direction of the relationship, was calculated to be -0.17, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.27, -0.06]. This suggests a statistical significance. 

The correlation coefficient was then converted into Cohen's d to obtain a standardised effect size to allow for comparison of effect sizes across universities and their subsequent pooling through a meta-analysis. The Cohen's d measure calculated to be -0.35, indicates a small to moderate effect size$^{3}$, suggesting that higher levels of statistics anxiety are associated with lower academic attainment at the University of Sussex. 

## Preliminary analysis continued: Brawijaya University

Brawijaya University Indonesia was then selected as a further case study, due to its vastly different grading system than the University of Sussex; using letter grades A - E. The grades were treated as ordered factors. Following data cleaning and filtering, 114 responses were retained. The mean STARS score was 71.2, with a standard deviation of 18.0 and a median of 72. Histograms were produced to further investigate the shape, spread and symmetry of the STARS score and grade.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 7, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Distributions of statistics anxiety and academic attainment at Brawijaya University."}
brawijaya_histograms()
```
Figure 3 shows the distribution of STARS Score is again approximately bell shaped and centered around a mean of 71.2. Most respondents achieved higher grades. The relationship between STARS score and academic attainment was then plotted.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, fig.cap="Boxplot of attainment vs statistical anxiety at Brawijaya University."}
brawijaya_relationship
```

It is not clear to tell if there is a correlation between STARS score and attainment. Spearman's correlation coefficient was calculated to be -0.07, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.25, 0.12]. This suggests a slight negative correlation, as in Sussex University, but the statistical significance can't be established yet. The Cohen's d was calculated to be -0.14, indicating a very weak negative correlation

## Extending analysis across universities

Having demonstrated the analytical approach using the University of Sussex and Brawijaya University, the same methodology was applied to the remaining universities to investigate whether the observed relationship between statistics anxiety and academic attainment was consistent across different universities and countries. 

Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was calculated independently for each university, alongside its corresponding 95% confidence interval. This method was used consistently across universities to accommodate differences in grading systems, particularly those with letter grades.

The correlation coefficients and their corresponding confidence intervals were subsequently converted into Cohen's d to obtain effect size estimates for the meta-analysis.

\begin{table}[H]
```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("effect_size_table.png")
```
\caption{Correlation and effect size information by universities.}
\end{table}

Table 2 shows that the effect size is only significant at the 95th level in 6 out of 18 universities, so at this point it was not possible to establish a cohesive result for all of the universities. Therefore, a meta-analysis, accounting for sample size, was conducted. This treated each university as a separate study and pooled the individual effect size estimates. 

## Meta-analysis

### Choice of meta-analysis model

There are two main approaches to pooling effect sizes: fixed effect (assumes  that one true effect size exists in the population) and random effect (assumes that the true effect varies).$^3$ Given the differences in educational settings, demographics, teaching methods and assessment systems across universities, a random effect model was chosen. 

### Pooling effect sizes

The standard error of each university's effect size was approximated using the width of its 95% confidence interval. The effect sizes were then pooled using a random-effects model implemented through the metafor package in R. 

A forest plot was produced to visualise the individual university effect sizes, their corresponding 95% confidence intervals and the overall pooled effect size.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 8, fig.cap="Forest plot of effect sizes across universities."}
meta_forest()
```

The pooled effect size was found to be -0.29, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.40,-0.18] and a standard error of 0.06, based on a total sample of 1,380 respondents across 18 universities. 

This suggests a small to moderate statistically significant negative effect, with the confidence interval not containing zero,. This indicates that the data is inconsistent with no association between statistics anxiety and attainment. It may be inferred that there is a correlation between students with higher statistics anxiety and students with lower attainment. 

It can be noted that some universities had very small sample sizes which produced variable estimates, such as the large confidence interval for Macquarie University as seen in Figure 5. These universities were retained as the meta-analysis weights studies with different sample sizes appropriately. 

### Heterogenity between universities

The test for heterogeneity, diversity between samples, was not statistically significant: $Q(df = 17) = 17.96, p= 0.39$. This indicates that the variation between the surveys in the different universities can be attributed to sampling error rather than true differences between universities, suggesting the negative relationship is consistent across different academic settings.$^4$

# Discussion and limitations

The aim of this investigation was to establish whether statistics anxiety is associated with academic attainment across universities. Whilst the preliminary analyses of the University of Sussex and Brawijaya University both indicated negative associations of varying degrees, the magnitude of the relationship varied across the wider dataset. The meta-analysis produced a pooled effect size of −0.29, indicating a small to moderate statistically significant negative association. These findings support the initial hypothesis that higher levels of statistics anxiety are associated with lower academic attainment.

Furthermore, the test for heterogeneity was not statistically significant, suggesting that the observed variation in effect sizes between universities is consistent with sampling error. Despite differences in teaching methods, assessment systems and student characteristics, there was insufficient evidence to suggest that the underlying relationship differed between universities. However, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this investigation.

One of the main limitations was the difference in grading systems across universities. Some universities used numerical grading methods, whilst others used letter-based grading systems. Although Spearman's rank correlation was used to account for these differences, the use of letter-based grades results in a loss of information compared with numerical grades. Students with different levels of attainment may be awarded the same letter grade and therefore assigned the same rank. This could affect the strength of the observed correlation, particularly when comparing universities with a limited number of grade categories to those using continuous numerical grading systems.

Selection bias may also have been introduced during the data cleaning process. Some universities reported students achieving grades of 0%, which were filtered out. These grades may have been recorded for multiple reasons, such as students genuinely achieving zero or failing to submit an assessment. By excluding these grades, students with particularly low attainment may be underrepresented in the analysis. Additional selection bias may have been introduced by excluding respondents who failed the attention checks or did not fully complete the anxiety questionnaires, as these students may differ systematically from those who were retained.

The universities included in this investigation span multiple continents, with questionnaires completed in seven different languages. The majority of students (67% of respondents) completed the questionnaire in English, whilst only 0.8% of respondents completed it in Hungarian. It could therefore be questioned whether the term 'statistics anxiety' and the individual questionnaire items are interpreted consistently across different languages and cultures.

Furthermore, the number of respondents varied considerably across universities, resulting in some effect size estimates being more precise than others. Although this was accounted for through inverse-variance weighting in the meta-analysis, universities with larger samples generally contributed more towards the pooled effect size. Consequently, the overall findings may not be equally representative of all universities and educational settings included in the investigation.

Respondents were also unevenly distributed across their year of study. Only 8% of respondents were in their third or fourth year of study at the time of completing the survey, with several more not revealing their year of study. With more data on respondents in later years, further investigation could be carried out into whether statistics anxiety differs according to year of study, as students may become more confident in their statistical knowledge as they progress through university.

The analysis did not account for additional variables that may influence both statistics anxiety and academic attainment, such as previous mathematical education, age, gender and degree subject. For example, students with a stronger mathematical background may experience lower levels of statistics anxiety whilst also achieving higher grades. Therefore, the observed relationship may be partially explained by factors other than statistics anxiety itself. Further research could incorporate these variables through multiple regression analysis.

A further limitation arises from the assumptions made during the meta-analysis. The individual survey groups were treated as independent studies, despite some universities contributing multiple survey groups. Students from the same university may share similar educational experiences, potentially challenging the assumption of independence. Furthermore, converting Spearman's rank correlation coefficients into Cohen's d and estimating standard errors from the transformed confidence intervals introduced additional approximations into the analysis.

Finally, whilst the research question investigates the effect of statistics anxiety on attainment, the observational nature of the SMARVUS dataset means that a causal relationship cannot be established. Although higher levels of statistics anxiety may negatively influence academic performance, previous experiences of poor academic performance may also contribute to increased anxiety. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted in terms of association rather tvhan causation.
